q: Which of these can be changed in place?
why: `bytearray` is the mutable counterpart of `bytes`, in the same way `list` is to `tuple`.

options: Four: one outer and three rows
Two: one outer and one row referenced three times
why: `[x] * n` repeats a reference. The outer list holds the same row three times, so writing to one row writes to all of them.

q: Which of these produces genuinely independent rows?
why: A comprehension evaluates its expression once per iteration, so each pass builds a new list.

options: Two keys with separate empty lists
Two keys pointing at one shared list
A TypeError, because the default is mutable
why: `fromkeys` is handed one already-built value and stores that same object against every key. It is `[x] * n` in dictionary form.
Lists implement `__iadd__`, so `+=` extends in place. Every name bound to that list sees the change.
Tuples have no `__iadd__`, so `+=` falls back to building a new tuple and rebinding. `b` never moved.

q: `dict(config)` where the values are lists gives you
options: A new dictionary holding the same list objects
A copy only of the keys
why: Every constructor-style copy in the standard library is shallow. The mapping is new; the values are shared.
The tuple guarantees which object each slot refers to. It makes no promise about that object's contents.

q: Why can `("a", "b")` be a dict key but `("a", [])` cannot?
options: Tuples of length two are special-cased
Hashability follows the contents, and a list is not hashable
The second one is longer in memory
It can, but only in Python 3.12 and later
why: A tuple's hash is computed from its elements, so it is hashable only if all of them are.

q: Deleting keys from a dict while looping over it
why: Dictionaries keep a version counter and their iterator checks it. A list in the same situation skips entries silently, which is worse.

q: `for x in items: items.remove(x)` on a list
options: Skips elements, because the index advances while the list shrinks
why: The loop walks an index forward through a sequence getting shorter underneath it. Sometimes the answer is right by luck, which is worse than always wrong.

options: A new sorted list, leaving the original alone
why: Throughout the standard library an in-place operation returns `None`, so chaining off it fails immediately rather than giving a silent wrong answer.

q: When is a function's default argument expression evaluated?
options: On every call that omits the argument
When the module is first garbage-collected
why: The result is stored on the function object, visible as `f.__defaults__`, and shared by every call for the life of the process.

q: Why `if into is None:` rather than `if not into:` for a sentinel default?
options: An empty list the caller deliberately passed is falsy and would be discarded
why: The sentinel test must distinguish "no argument given" from "an argument that happens to be empty".

q: A function both mutates its argument and returns it. What is wrong with that?
options: Nothing; it is the most convenient form
It invites the caller to treat the result as a new object when it is the same one
It prevents the function from being annotated
why: Pick one: mutate and return `None`, or leave the input alone and return something new.
